newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Army said looking at more than 300 sex cases.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Army said looking at more than 300 sex cases.

text.p: Army officials said Thursday they were investigating more than 300 allegations of sexual harassment or rape and indirectly denied a new charge that investigators coerced women to make false rape charges.
They released summary figures at a briefing showing that 1,187 allegations of sexual harassment made to a special Army telephone hotline have resulted in 291 criminal investigations so far.

The summary said investigations of 387 of the allegations had been closed, indicating no wrongdoing was found, 36 had been referred to other agencies and 273 were undergoing preliminary investigation.

In addition to the hotline investigations, an official said, Army agents have investigated about 100 complaints against 22 drill sergeants and other soldiers at Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland, and about 20 soldiers at Fort Leonard Wood, Missouri.
He said Army headquarters did not know the total number of sexual harassment or rape charges being investigated at other U.S. Army installations around the world.
The investigations at Aberdeen have led to charges of rape against a captain and three drill sergeants or instructors and lesser sexual harassment charges against four others.

The Army officials, briefing reporters on Army criminal investigation procedures on condition they not be identified, said they could not talk about specific cases but indirectly denied an allegation they tried to coerce rape charges.

Five women trainees at Aberdeen said at a news conference Tuesday that investigators pressured them to accuse instructors of rape after they admitted having consensual sex with the instructors. Four said they refused to charge rape. The fifth said she accused a sergeant of sexual misconduct but later recanted.
But the Army officials said Thursday that in the military, just as in civilian courts, no one could be charged with rape unless they threatened death or physical injury to get sex.
They said an Army drill sergeant who used his power to threaten to destroy a woman's Army career if she did not have sex with him would be charged with sexual harassment, not rape.

The officials said Army investigators simply took witnesses' statements without coercion. They said if it became evident the witness might be guilty of a crime, which in the military included illicit sex with a superior, the interview must be stopped and the witness advised of his or her right to say nothing further without a lawyer present.
